old: Estimates are around 6 million or more, much less documented than the Atlantic trade.
new: Paul Lovejoy’s widely cited estimates total roughly 11 million (about 7.4 million across the Sahara and 3–4 million via the Red Sea and East Africa); others are lower. It is much less documented than the Atlantic trade.
problem: The item cites Lovejoy, whose estimates total about 10.7–11.5 million (7.42 million trans-Saharan plus 3.3–4.0 million Red Sea/East Africa), so ‘around 6 million or more’ badly understates the cited scholarship.
sources: Boston University African Studies Center, Slave Trade Tables (from Lovejoy, Transformations in Slavery, 3rd ed. 2012): https://www.bu.edu/africa/files/2023/11/Slave-Trade-Tables.docx.pdf

old: In 1994 extremists killed an estimated 500,000–800,000 people, mostly Tutsi,
new: In 1994 extremists killed an estimated 500,000 to about 1 million people (the UN and Rwanda’s government say about 1 million), mostly Tutsi,
problem: The range stops at 800,000 while citing the UN, which (like Rwanda’s government census) puts the toll at about 1 million; the low-end scholarly range is presented as the whole picture.
sources: UN Secretary-General message, 7 April 2024: ‘Over the course of 100 days, 1 million people were killed.’ https://press.un.org/en/2024/sgsm22184.doc.htm

old: became a decade of civil war that killed up to about a million people.
new: became a decade of civil war that caused over a million deaths (demographer Robert McCaa estimates about 1.4 million excess deaths).
problem: ‘Up to about a million’ presents a ceiling that is below the leading demographic estimate (McCaa 2003: about 1.4 million excess deaths, 2.1 million total population loss).
sources: Robert McCaa, ‘Missing millions: the demographic costs of the Mexican Revolution’, Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos 19:2 (2003): https://users.pop.umn.edu/~rmccaa/missmill/abstract.htm
